articles.author: Joshua Partlow
articles.summary: For four and a half hours, the sky above the United States emptied out. Normally, throughout the day and the night, thousands of planes are taking off, crisscrossing the country, and landing. When the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all U.S. flights around 4:00 p.m. today, because of “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” some 4,000 airplanes were in the sky, headed for U.S. airports, according to Flightradar24, an aviation-tracking website. Even if no more flights took off, all of those planes needed to land. For the people below, getting them down safely became an immediate preoccupation. This type of nationwide grounding had happened only twice before in recent history—once after the September 11 attacks, and once in January 2023 for about an hour and a half. Every aircraft still aloft needed to make it to its destination, despite apparently spotty communications. Our formidable system of flight, a machine that’s constantly in motion and choreographed to the minute, has backups built in. articles.summary: Behind the Mississippi senator-elect’s victory is a coalition of groups that didn’t have a lot of money, but had collective power and post-Callais anger Long before national political leaders and media were paying any attention, long before the Louisiana v Callais supreme court decision gutted the Voting Rights Act, Mississippi organizers were working to grow political participation and improve quality of life in a state that often ranks low on its residents’ health and wellbeing. Activists’ momentum contributed to Democrat Scott Colom’s historic upset in the midterm elections. A loose coalition of about a dozen, mostly Black-led nonprofits or initiatives rallied residents after Callais, the April decision that set off a flurry of redistricting efforts across southern states. That case was not the sole impetus for organizing efforts across Mississippi, but it turned out thousands in the 20 May “Mississippi Fights Back” rally . articles.author: Ashley Gold
articles.summary: Democrats are facing heavy pressure from AI safety groups to ramp up oversight of the Trump administration’s AI policy when they take power next year, according to two letters shared first with Semafor. The AI accountability group Guardrails Action and nine other groups wrote to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, arguing that voters were clear in the midterms that they want AI and government accountability. The groups seized on the recent Nvidia controversy, demanding hearings with now-former CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Department officials. “The concentration of power and wealth from AI, and the risks that come with it, are historic. Countering that power is the most important fight of our lifetime,” the letter reads. A second letter from the Alliance for Secure AI and the Tech Oversight Project addresses Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick directly, demanding he support strengthened export controls.
